Empirical Research Plan: Do U.K. MPs reap private financial returns from winning a seat? Does the return differ by party?

---------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------
Method: Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the vote-margin cutoff in the candidate’s first general election (Lee 2008 style).

Why appropriate
•	“Winners” and “runners-up” in very tight races are as-good-as random draws of otherwise identical individuals.  
•	Winning a seat is a large, discrete jump in access to the levers of political influence, while the running variable (win margin) is continuous and cannot be perfectly manipulated ex-ante.  
•	Outcomes (estate value at death, number of paid directorships, etc.) are measured long after the treatment, so reverse causality is implausible.

We can augment the RD with a fuzzy-IV interpretation in which the first-stage is “win seat → years served in Parliament.”  The reduced-form RD gives the local average treatment effect (LATE) of winning; the IV ratio gives the effect of an additional year in Parliament.

---------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------
Running variable:  
vote_margin = (candidate vote share – closest opponent vote share) in the *first* election the candidate contests.

Cutoff: 0 percentage points.

Treatment definition:  
Treated = 1{vote_margin ≥ 0} (candidate wins seat the first time).

Control: 1{vote_margin < 0} (candidate narrowly loses).

Timing: The “event” occurs on election night of the first contest (1950–1970 cohorts). Outcomes are realised over the life-cycle and measured at death (estate value) or in 1975/1983/1990/2007 for outside interests.

Heterogeneity: Interact treatment with Conservative dummy (CON=1, LAB=0).  Estimate separate bandwidth-optimal local linear RDs by party, or pool and interact.

---------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff.  
 Plausibility: Strong. Candidates cannot perfectly predict *exact* vote margin; small idiosyncratic shocks (weather on polling day, ballot order, local events) drive razor-thin results.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
 Plausibility: High. UK election administration is centralised; recounts are automatic; fraud at the one-vote margin is historically negligible. We will run the McCrary (density) test.

A3. Covariates evolve smoothly through the cutoff.  
 Plausibility: Likely, but testable. Check balance in age, occupation, schooling, baseline titles, prior wealth proxies.

A4. Local SUTVA: one candidate’s margin does not affect another’s prospective estate except through that candidate winning.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable in single-member districts.

A5. Stable composition: mortality selection unrelated to vote margin within the bandwidth.  
 Plausibility: Some concern; winners may have better health care access.  We can test for differential survival length.

---------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
---------------------------------------------------
T1. Sorting/manipulation of close races.  
 •	Diagnostic: McCrary test on win margin density; placebo RD on pre-treatment covariates.  
 •	Mitigation: Use donut RD (drop ±0.5 pp), local randomisation checks.

T2. Differential attrition or measurement error in probate values (e.g., missing estates for early deaths before 1984 registry).  
 •	Diagnostic: RD on probability estate recorded.  
 •	Mitigation: Inverse-probability weighting; Lee bounds; restrict to cohorts whose death is observable.

T3. Pre-existing wealth differences correlated with vote margin (rich candidates may run in safer seats yet still be near cutoff).  
 •	Data: Pre-treatment occupation, titled status, secondary school, and Oxbridge flag as proxies for baseline SES.  
 •	Mitigation: Include covariates in RD; test covariate balance; use residualised outcomes.

---------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------
```r
# Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)
library(fixest)

# 1. Load and clean -------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("uk_candidates_1950_1970.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    vote_margin = vote_share - opponent_share,        # running variable
    win = if_else(vote_margin >= 0, 1, 0),
    estate_real = estate_value_2007_gbp,
    cons = if_else(party == "Conservative", 1, 0)
  ) %>%
  filter(abs(vote_margin) <= 10)   # keep races within ±10 p.p. for RD universe

# 2. Main RD: Full sample -----------------------------------------------
rd_full <- rdrobust(
  y = df$estate_real,
  x = df$vote_margin,
  covs = df %>% select(age, oxbridge, titled, occupation_professional),
  fuzzy = NULL          # sharp RD
)

print(summary(rd_full))

# 3. Party-specific RD ----------------------------------------------------
rd_con  <- rdrobust(y = df$estate_real[df$cons==1],
                    x = df$vote_margin[df$cons==1])

rd_lab  <- rdrobust(y = df$estate_real[df$cons==0],
                    x = df$vote_margin[df$cons==0])

# 4. Fuzzy IV: effect per year in Parliament -----------------------------
df <- df %>%
  mutate(years_mp = if_else(win==1, years_served, 0))

rd_fuzzy <- rdrobust(
  y = df$estate_real,
  x = df$vote_margin,
  fuzzy = df$years_mp
)

# 5. Robustness: Donut RD (drop ±0.5 p.p.) -------------------------------
df_donut <- df %>% filter(abs(vote_margin) > 0.5)

rd_donut <- rdrobust(y = df_donut$estate_real,
                     x = df_donut$vote_margin)

# 6. Covariate balance & McCrary test (visual) ---------------------------
balance <- feols(age + oxbridge + titled ~ win | 0, data = df, cluster = vote_margin)
summary(balance)

rddensity(df$vote_margin)$tests
```

---------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------
Theory: Access to policy influence should translate into lucrative consultancies and boards, especially for Conservatives with business ties. Labour MPs face union monitoring and lower market demand for influence.

Prior:  
•	Conservative winners ≈ 20–30 percent higher probate wealth (≈ £150k–£250k in 2007 GBP) than narrow losers.  
•	Labour winners ≈ 0–10 percent, possibly indistinguishable from zero.  
Overall pooled effect ≈ 10–15 percent.

---------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
---------------------------------------------------
C1. No precise manipulation of running variable……… 1  
C2. Covariate balance near cutoff…………………………….. 1  
C3. Functional form correctly specified……………………… 0.5 (we use data-driven bandwidths but form risk exists)  
C4. No other discontinuities at cutoff………………………… 0.5 (survival & data capture must be checked)  
C5. Sufficient observations close to cutoff………………… 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 ⇒ reasonably credible but contingent on robustness tests.

---------------------------------------------------
This plan yields a transparent, replicable estimate of the personal financial return to Parliamentary office and how it differs across Britain’s two major post-war parties.
